summary: 18 claims, all fetched and re-checked against the raw text (PDFs were read as text from the downloaded files; regulations were read on two sites). Wind ladder in km/h, my conversions from the printed figures: 20 mph is 32 (OSHA, lifting people), 38 (Abu Dhabi, stop all lifting), 12.5 m/s is 45 (typical outdoor platform rating), 17 m/s is 61 (UK crane practice), 20 m/s is 72 (normal crane design), 28.5 m/s is 103 (process cranes). Key facts: wind can rise from 13 to 20 m/s in about 20 minutes (UK CPA note); the OSHA crane rules I read (1926.1417, 1926.1431, 1926.1435) give one wind number, 20 mph for lifting people; the lightning rule is 30 minutes after the last thunder and no system can detect the first strike; hot work uses a 35-ft radius, a 60-minute fire watch (NFPA) and a 10 percent LEL gas test (OSHA shipyard rule); a confined space permit must log test results with tester and time (item 10 of 15); Piper Alpha killed 167 with possible permit failings identified; heat stress contributed to 18% of 629 crane operator injuries; heat waves raised driver-performance crashes by 7.7%. Also verified but not in the 18: HSE says winds above 23mph (Force 5) affect balance; OSHA 1926.451(f)(12) has no scaffold wind number; AAA Foundation says an estimated 17.6% of US fatal crashes in 2017-2021 involved a drowsy driver (https://aaafoundation.org/drowsy-driving-in-fatal-crashes-united-states-2017-2021/); overtime jobs carry a 61% higher injury hazard rate, 12-hour days 37% and 60-hour weeks 23% (Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 2005, 10,793 US participants, 1987-2000; Europe PMC record fetched by title: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE:%22impact%20of%20overtime%20and%20long%20work%20hours%20on%20occupational%20injuries%22&resultType=core&format=json). Gulf anchors are the Abu Dhabi lifting code and the Mecca 2015 crane collapse (sensitive). The web search budget ran out mid-run, so no Saudi permit or wind rule was found.

claims.topic: Wind limit for lifting people by crane (OSHA)
claims.figure: 20 mph (sustained or gusts) at the personnel platform
claims.measures: Wind speed above which a qualified person must decide whether lifting people by crane is unsafe. If it is not safe, the lift must not begin, or must be terminated if under way. Paragraph 1926.1431(k)(8)(i). Paragraph (k)(8)(ii) adds a separate duty to stop for dangerous weather or other danger. Exact wording also checked at https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.1431. Same subpart, no wind number in the tower crane or operation rules: 1926.1435(b)(4)(iii) says wind must not exceed the speed recommended by the manufacturer (or set by a qualified person if none), and 1926.1435(e)(6)(v) requires a wind speed indicator mounted above the upper rotating structure of a tower crane (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.1435). 1926.1417(h) and (n) only ask the competent person to act on storm warnings and to adjust for wind (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.1417).
claims.source_title: 29 CFR 1926.1431 Hoisting personnel (Subpart CC, Cranes and Derricks in Construction)
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
claims.quote: When wind speed (sustained or gusts) exceeds 20 mph at the personnel platform, a qualified person must determine if...
claims.use_in_story: Show a wind gauge crossing 20 mph and a person-lift permit flipping from green to hold.

claims.figure: In-service design wind speed 14 m/s (125 N/m2) for cranes easily secured and used in light winds only; 20 m/s (250 N/m2) for all normal cranes installed in the open; 28,5 m/s (500 N/m2) for cranes in process applications
claims.measures: Clause 5.1, Table 2 (printed page 3, PDF page 7). Wind speed is measured at the highest point of the crane. The table assumes the crane can be fully secured before the design wind speed is reached, so securing must start at a lower wind speed. Clause 6 covers out-of-service wind and the scope says the standard gives guidance on when to secure the crane. My conversions: 14 m/s is 50 km/h, 20 m/s is 72 km/h, 28.5 m/s is 103 km/h. The copy read is a free preview hosted by a standards reseller, not the ISO web store.
claims.source_title: ISO 4302:2016 Cranes - Wind load assessment (preview copy)
claims.publisher: International Organization for Standardization (ISO); preview hosted by iTeh Standards
claims.quote: The wind speed shall be measured at the highest point of the crane.
claims.use_in_story: Use the three design speeds as rungs on a wind ladder and show the sensor at the crane top, not on the ground.

claims.topic: Tower crane wind limit in practice (UK industry note citing BS 7121)
claims.figure: Design in-service limit 20m/s (45mph/72kmh); industry practice limit 17m/s (38mph/61kmh); vacuum lifter 8m/s (18mph/28kmh); large shutter 7m/s (16mph/25kmh)
claims.measures: Page 2. The lower 17 m/s figure leaves time to put the crane into its out-of-service condition. The note says the load-area reduction formula is in Annex D-1 of BS 7121-1:2016 and EN 13000. Page 10: a tower crane operator should not remain in the cab above 20m/s (45mph). The note also gives a practical upper limit of 31mph for mobile cranes with non-wind-sensitive loads (page 12, citing its sister note CIG TIN 101). The note prints both 72kmh and 75kmh for 20m/s in different places; 72 is the correct conversion. BS 7121 itself is paywalled and was not read.
claims.source_title: TIN CIG/TCIG 110 Planning and Control of Lifting Operations in Wind
claims.publisher: Construction Plant-hire Association (CPA), Crane and Tower Crane Interest Groups
claims.quote: tower crane's design in-service wind speed limit is 20m/s (45mph/72kmh) but industry generally limits it to 17m/s (38mph/61kmh)
claims.use_in_story: Animate a tower crane with a wind dial that has a design line at 20 m/s and an earlier amber line at 17 m/s.

claims.topic: How fast wind builds and when lifting may restart (UK industry note citing BS 7121-5)
claims.figure: About 20 minutes for wind to rise from 13m/s (30mph/47kmh) to 20m/s (45mph/75kmh); tower crane back in service only after wind below the limit for at least 10 minutes; common practice is to wait 30 minutes
claims.measures: Page 1 gives the 20-minute rise as a rule of thumb or approximation. Page 10, section 4.2: a tower crane should not be put back into service until the wind has been lower than the in-service or load limit for at least 10 minutes, a principle the note attributes to BS7121-5:2019 14.1.4.2. Page 10, section 4.3: it is common practice to wait 30 minutes after the wind drops below the threshold, and the timer resets if the threshold is exceeded again. Page 3: forecasts are given at 10m height for a 10km x 10km grid square; crane design and wind-off decisions use the 3-second peak gust while general forecasts use a 10-minute mean; height factors from a Liebherr table are 1.181 at 50m, 1.272 at 100m and 1.329 at 150m. Page 10: many apps only revise their forecast twice a day. So a site sensor at crane height gives data a forecast cannot.
claims.source_title: TIN CIG/TCIG 110 Planning and Control of Lifting Operations in Wind
claims.publisher: Construction Plant-hire Association (CPA), Crane and Tower Crane Interest Groups
claims.quote: it is estimated that it takes on average 20 minutes for the wind to rise from 13m/s (30mph/47kmh) to 20m/s (45mph/75kmh)
claims.use_in_story: Show wind climbing from 13 to 20 m/s in about 20 minutes with a 10-minute and 30-minute restart timer, so the alert must be automatic.

claims.topic: Abu Dhabi stop-work wind speed for lifting (Gulf)
claims.figure: 38 km/h (20.5) knots: lifting operations must cease at this recorded wind speed or gusts
claims.measures: Clause 3.6.6(e), page 12 of 24. Same clause: (a) an anemometer on each worksite where cranes are used, fitted at the highest point of the crane where reasonably practicable, with handheld units only as a secondary check at ground level; (b) provisions to determine wind direction; (c) the manufacturer wind-off speed communicated to the operator and appointed person; (d) meteorological reports obtained at least daily. Clause 3.8.1(a)(x), page 14: where a tower crane has an anemometer, a repeater must be fitted at the base of the crane or in the project site office. Clause 3.10.1(a)(ix), page 18: MEWP wind speeds shall be monitored and the wind-off speed follows the manufacturer. The code applies to all employers in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi (clause 1(a)). My conversion: 38 km/h is about 10.6 m/s or 23.6 mph. The sister code CoP 23.0 Working at Height v4.1 (Feb 2026) has no wind or weather limit (text search of the downloaded PDF). Neither code mentions lightning.
claims.source_title: ADOSH-SF Code of Practice CoP 34.0 Safe Use of Lifting Equipment and Lifting Accessories, Version 4.1
claims.publisher: Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre (ADPHC), OSHAD system framework
claims.quote: In all cases employers shall ensure that lifting operations cease when the recorded wind speed reaches or gusts in excess of 38 km/h (20.5) knots.
claims.use_in_story: Use as the Gulf anchor: a hard stop at 38 km/h, with the site weather station feeding the same number into the lift permit.

claims.figure: 28mph (12.5m/s) maximum wind rating for a typical outdoor MEWP, measured at the platform
claims.measures: Page 1: the rating must be shown on the data plate and at the control position; indoor-only machines carry 0 m/s; the 12.5 m/s wind is applied in the stability design; wind at height may be stronger than at ground level. Page 2: IPAF recommends a handheld anemometer at the work platform. Work at height context: HSE says winds in excess of 23mph (Force 5) will affect a persons balance (https://www.hse.gov.uk/construction/faq-height.htm, answer to 'Is there a wind speed above which roofing work should stop?'). OSHA 1926.451(f)(12) bans scaffold work in storms or high winds unless a competent person finds it safe and workers have fall arrest or wind screens, with no wind number (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.451). My conversion: 12.5 m/s is 45 km/h and 23 mph is 37 km/h.
claims.region: International (IPAF guidance, North American standards context)
claims.year: 2020 (inferred from document code TE-1092-0620; file uploaded 2021-12 per URL)
claims.source_title: Wind Rating: Using MEWPs in Wind (TE-1092-0620-1-en-US)
claims.quote: Typically, an outdoor-rated MEWP has a maximum wind rating of 28mph (12.5m/s).
claims.use_in_story: Link each platform's own wind rating to the equipment record so a wind alert can name the machines that must come down.

claims.topic: Lightning rule for outdoor work, cranes and power work (OSHA and NOAA)
claims.figure: Stay in shelter at least 30 minutes after the last thunder; lightning can strike up to 10 miles from any rainfall
claims.measures: Page 2 (30 minutes) and page 1 (10 miles). Page 1 lists heavy equipment operation, construction (e.g. scaffolding), power utility field repair, steel erection and roofing among higher-risk work. Page 2 captions a crane photo 'Cranes are especially vulnerable to lightning.' Page 3: no systems can detect the first strike, detect all lightning, or predict lightning strikes. The emergency action plan should say when to suspend and when to resume outdoor work and the time needed to reach shelter. NWS adds that lightning can strike outward 10 miles from a thunderstorm so hearing thunder means you are likely within striking distance (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-overview) and that lightning kills about 20 people a year in the US (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-victims). NWS analysis for 2006 to 2019: 18% of 418 US lightning deaths were work-related, of which construction 21% and roofing 17% (https://www.weather.gov/media/safety/Analysis06-19.pdf, pages 1 and 8). OSHA 1926.1417, the crane operation rule, has no lightning wording (checked on two copies), so no crane regulation read here sets a lightning rule.
claims.source_title: Lightning Safety When Working Outdoors (OSHA fact sheet FS-3863)
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) with NOAA National Weather Service
claims.quote: Remain in the shelter for at least 30 minutes after hearing the last sound of thunder.
claims.use_in_story: Run a 30-minute timer that restarts on every thunder alert, and say plainly that sensors warn but cannot predict the first strike.

claims.figure: 35-ft (11-m) radius cleared of combustibles; fire watch on site for a minimum of 60 minutes after the work
claims.measures: Fact sheet page 2, summarising NFPA 51B 2019 edition. The permit authorizing individual may require a longer fire watch. The NFPA 51B text itself was not read. Contrast: OSHA fact sheet 4188 (Sept 2022) says fire watches must continue for at least 30 minutes after hot work and that NFPA 51B recommends monitoring for up to an additional 3 hours as determined by the permit authorizing individual (https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA4188.pdf, page 3). OSHA general industry 1910.252(a)(2)(iii) uses 35 feet (10.7 m) and a half hour (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.252).
claims.quote: The fire watch must remain on site for a minimum of 60 minutes to monitor for smoldering fires, per NFPA 51B.
claims.use_in_story: Animate a 35-ft circle around a hot work tag and a 60-minute fire watch timer that starts when the permit closes.

claims.figure: 4,580 structure fires a year; 22 civilian deaths, 171 civilian injuries and $484M direct property damage a year; 5 firefighter fatalities between 2001-2018
claims.measures: Fact sheet page 1, quoting the 2021 NFPA report 'Hot Work Structure Fires' for 2014-2018 data. 57% of the fires were in or on non-home properties and 43% in homes. The numbers exclude near-miss fires handled by the fire watch.
claims.quote: 4,580 Structure fires involving hot work per year
claims.use_in_story: Show the four yearly numbers as counters beside a hot work permit card.

claims.figure: 2 firefighters killed in March 2014; cause: unpermitted welding where high winds and nearby combustible material were not taken into account
claims.measures: Fact sheet page 1, case study 'Partnering for Safety'. The sentence names two fatalities (a firefighter and a lieutenant); names left out here on purpose. The city then required a hot work safety certificate and Massachusetts adopted a similar rule effective July 1, 2018.
claims.quote: unpermitted welding, where the workers did not take factors such as high winds and nearby combustible material into account
claims.use_in_story: Show wind speed as a visible condition on the hot work permit card.

claims.topic: Deaths from hot work on tanks and the gas monitoring lesson
claims.figure: Over 60 fatalities since 1990 from explosions and fires during hot work on tanks
claims.measures: CSB news release dated March 4, 2010 (page 2) about its bulletin 'Seven Key Lessons to Prevent Worker Deaths During Hot Work In and Around Tanks'. The release says combustible gas monitors read as a percentage of the lower explosive limit, that the absence of flammables needs to be verified before and during any hot work, and that OSHA did not require combustible gas monitoring for hot work on or near flammable storage tanks (a statement made in March 2010; rules may have changed). CSB fact sheet April 2018 lists lesson 3 (monitor the atmosphere with a calibrated combustible gas detector before and during hot work) and lesson 5 (use written permits that name the work and the precautions): https://www.csb.gov/assets/1/6/csb_cdl_factsheet_-_hot_work.pdf.
claims.source_title: News release: Following Deadly Explosion at PCA Corrugated Mill in Wisconsin, CSB Issues Safety Bulletin on Hazards of Welding and Other Hot Work
claims.publisher: US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB)
claims.quote: the CSB has identified over 60 fatalities since 1990 due to explosions and fires from hot work activities on tanks.
claims.use_in_story: Pair the 60-plus deaths with a gas reading in percent LEL on the hot work permit, checked before and during the job.

claims.topic: Hot work gas test threshold (OSHA shipyard rule)
claims.figure: No flammable vapor concentration equal to or greater than 10 percent of the lower explosive limit
claims.measures: Paragraph 1915.14(b)(1): hot work is not permitted in dry cargo holds, bilges, certain engine and boiler spaces, vessel sections and land-side confined or enclosed spaces until a competent person has tested and found the atmosphere below that level. Wording confirmed on osha.gov and law.cornell.edu. This is the shipyard standard. It is not taken from NFPA 51B, whose text was not read.
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
claims.quote: determined to contain no concentrations of flammable vapors equal to or greater than 10 percent of the lower explosive limit
claims.use_in_story: Show a gas gauge with a red line at 10 percent LEL gating the hot work permit.

claims.figure: 15 required permit items, including (f)(10) results of initial and periodic tests with tester names or initials and time; oxygen is hazardous below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent
claims.measures: Paragraph 1910.146(f)(1) to (f)(15). Item (f)(15) links other permits, such as hot work, issued for work in the space. The permit duration may not exceed the time needed for the task, paragraph (e)(4). Test order in (d)(5)(iii): oxygen first, then combustible gases and vapors, then toxic gases and vapors. Oxygen limits are in the definition of hazardous atmosphere, item (3). Wording read on osha.gov and law.cornell.edu (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.146).
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
claims.quote: The results of initial and periodic tests performed under paragraph (d)(5) of this section, accompanied by the names or initials of the testers
claims.use_in_story: Show the gas sensor writing time-stamped readings straight into the permit, as item 10 requires.

claims.topic: Permit-to-work failure in a major disaster (Piper Alpha, 1988)
claims.figure: 167 men lost their lives; possible failings in the permit to work system were identified as an element in the disaster
claims.measures: UK House of Commons Hansard, 12 November 1990, statement by the Secretary of State for Energy on the public inquiry report: sympathy for the 167 men who lost their lives, and his department's technical investigation identified possible failings in the operator's permit to work system. Hansard 7 March 1991 debate: 226 men were on the platform on the night of 6 July 1988 and only 61 of those men survived (https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1991/mar/07/piper-alpha-cullen-report). Do not say 167 of 226: the sources give the two figures separately. HSE guidance HSG250 (2005), PDF page 6, reminds readers of the importance of permit-to-work failures in the sequence of events leading to Piper Alpha; case study 4 (page 9) says there was no cross-referencing between permits and reliance was placed on memory; case study 12 (page 13) says handovers failed to communicate that PSV 504 (a pressure safety valve) had been removed for overhaul; case study 6 (page 10) says a 1989 vapour cloud explosion at a chemical complex in the USA killed 23 people and injured 300, with no effective permit-to-work system covering both employees and contractors (https://books.hse.gov.uk/gempdf/hsg250.pdf). The Cullen report itself was not read.
claims.source_title: Piper Alpha, House of Commons debate 12 November 1990 (Hansard); HSE HSG250 Guidance on permit-to-work systems
claims.publisher: UK Parliament (Hansard); Health and Safety Executive (HSE) for HSG250
claims.quote: identified possible failings in the generation of [the operator's] permit to work system as an element in the disaster
claims.use_in_story: Show two permits on one pump that never cross-reference, then the figure 167, to make the case for one linked permit record.

claims.figure: Heat stress contributed to 18% of the 629 personal injuries reported by crane operators; 75% of 2,170 certified crane personnel said heat stress or illness was likely or very likely
claims.measures: Page 5, Figure 2 (operators 18%, n=629; riggers 24%; trainers 24%; supervisors 21%). Page 3: 2023 Work to Zero and NCCCO Foundation survey of 2,170 NCCCO-certified field personnel; heat stress was the leading systemic risk factor for personal injuries (18%) and for injuries to others on site (16%). Page 5 says heat can impair focus, reaction time and communication accuracy of signalpersons. US data, no Gulf equivalent found.
claims.source_title: Addressing Heat Stress in the Crane Industry
claims.publisher: National Safety Council (NSC) with the NCCCO Foundation
claims.quote: among crane operators, heat stress contributed to 18% of the 629 reported personal injuries
claims.use_in_story: Show a crane cab with a heat index dial and the 18 percent figure beside it.

claims.topic: Heat and crash risk for drivers
claims.figure: +2.9% crash risk on heat-wave days; +7.7% for crashes with driver performance factors on heat-wave days; +1.1% per 1 °C of maximum temperature for those crashes
claims.measures: 118,489 motor vehicle crashes with victims, warm periods 2000-2011, Catalonia (an average of 64.1 per day). Driver performance factors are distractions, driver error, fatigue or sleepiness. Temperature came from 66 weather stations. 95% confidence intervals: 0.7% to 5.1% (all crashes, heat waves), 1.2% to 14.6% (driver performance, heat waves), 0.1% to 2.1% (driver performance, per 1 °C). DOI 10.1289/ehp.1409223. Read as the Europe PMC abstract record of the paper.
claims.source_title: High Ambient Temperatures and Risk of Motor Vehicle Crashes in Catalonia, Spain (2000-2011): A Time-Series Analysis
claims.quote: The estimated risk of crashes significantly increased by 2.9% [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.7%, 5.1%] during heat wave days
claims.use_in_story: Show heat-wave days as a bump on a driver crash-risk line, with the 7.7 percent fatigue-type figure called out.

claims.topic: Fatigue compared with alcohol impairment (operators and drivers)
claims.figure: After 17-19 hours without sleep, performance on some tests equal to or worse than blood alcohol 0.05%; after longer, equal to 0.1%; response speeds up to 50% slower on some tests
claims.measures: 39 subjects (30 transport industry employees and nine from the army) tested over 28 hours of sleep deprivation and after alcohol doses up to about 0.1% blood alcohol concentration. In the study 17-19 hours without sleep corresponds to 2230 and 0100. The abstract does not state the country. DOI 10.1136/oem.57.10.649. Read as the Europe PMC abstract record of the paper.
claims.region: Not stated in the abstract (transport industry employees and army personnel)
claims.source_title: Moderate sleep deprivation produces impairments in cognitive and motor performance equivalent to legally prescribed levels of alcohol intoxication
claims.quote: After 17-19 hours without sleep, corresponding to 2230 and 0100, performance on some tests was equivalent or worse than that at a BAC of 0.05%.
claims.use_in_story: Set hours on shift beside a blood-alcohol scale to show why long shifts need rest rules.

claims.topic: Gulf lifting incident in a storm (Mecca, 2015)
claims.figure: At least 107 killed and 238 wounded (initial official toll); later reports give between 108 and 111 killed
claims.measures: Al Jazeera, 12 September 2015: Saudi Civil Defence Authority toll; a Saudi Press Agency spokesperson said the crane was brought down by strong wind and heavy rain. Later sources differ on the toll: Fox News (January 2017) says the collapse killed 111 pilgrims (https://www.foxnews.com/world/saudi-court-drops-case-over-crane-collapse-that-killed-111.amp); The National (15 February 2023) says at least 109 were killed and that the Criminal Court of Appeal found the company guilty of negligence and safety breaches and fined it 20 million riyals (https://www.thenationalnews.com/gulf-news/2023/02/15/saudi-court-fines-binladin-firm-sr20m-in-2015-crane-crash-case/). Gulf News (which gives 108 killed and 238 injured) reports an earlier 2017 acquittal that blamed heavy rain and thunderstorms (https://gulfnews.com/world/gulf/saudi/saudi-arabia-mecca-court-acquits-13-defendants-in-grand-mosque-crane-collapse-1.1607538811891). Courts changed their view over time, so do not present wind as the only cause. Sensitive event; review before use.
claims.source_title: Saudi crane collapse kills 107 in Mecca Grand Mosque
claims.publisher: Al Jazeera (quoting the Saudi Civil Defence Authority and the Saudi Press Agency)
claims.quote: the crane was brought down by strong wind and heavy rain
claims.use_in_story: Say more than 100 people died when a crane fell in a storm at the Grand Mosque in 2015, and do not state a single cause.

gaps: WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200 calls) during the run, so discovery stopped. Saudi-specific wind, lightning or permit rules (Aramco, Royal Commission for Jubail and Yanbu, Saudi Building Code) and other Gulf states (Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain, Dubai) were not found. Only Abu Dhabi (OSHAD) and the Mecca 2015 incident cover the Gulf.
ASME B30.3 and B30.5 and the full BS 7121 text are paywalled. BS 7121 figures (Annex D-1 formula, 10-minute restart in BS 7121-5:2019 14.1.4.2) come only through the UK CPA note, a secondary source.

The NFPA 51B text itself was not read. Its 35 ft and 60 minute figures come from the NFPA 2021 fact sheet. The numeric hot work gas test (10 percent LEL) comes from OSHA shipyard rule 1915.14, not from NFPA 51B. No NFPA 51B gas test figure was obtained.

OSHA 1926.1417, 1926.1435 and 1926.451(f)(12) give no numeric wind limit. The word lightning was not found in 1926.1417 (two copies, model-assisted check, not a literal text search). OSHAD CoP 34.0 and CoP 23.0 (v4.1, Feb 2026) contain no lightning wording and CoP 23.0 has no wind or weather limit (text search of the downloaded PDFs).

Electrical work and lightning: no standard was found that ties an electrical permit to lightning. HSE HSG85 (2013) has no lightning or weather wording (text search) and a Cornell LII check of OSHA 1910.269 found none. Only the OSHA and NOAA fact sheet lists power utility field repair as higher risk.

Permit-to-work causation: the Cullen report itself was not read (HSE hosts it as large PDFs). The 167 figure comes from UK Hansard, not from HSE pages. No HSE statistic on the share of incidents with a permit-to-work failure was found.

Heat and equipment operators or drivers: no Gulf figure found. A 2026 truck-driver telematics paper (Journal of Environmental Economics and Management, 'Too hot to haul') could not be fetched (HTTP 403), so it is not used. The NHTSA drowsy driving page also returned HTTP 403.

Mecca 2015: the toll differs by source (107, 108, 109, 111 killed) and courts reversed their findings (acquittal 2017, negligence finding 2023). Treat the event as sensitive and do not name a cause or a company.
ISO 4302 was read from a free preview copy hosted by a standards reseller, not from the ISO store. IPAF guidance has no explicit date, the year 2020 is inferred from its document code.
OSHA fact sheet FS-3863 (06/2021) still carries an older 'about 50 deaths a year over 30 years' figure. NWS now says about 20 a year, so use the NWS number.
